content: Comprehensive national immunization plans should be developed as part of broader national health strategies, using a collaborative, bottom-up approach that involves all stakeholders. Ambitious yet achievable country-specific targets should be set, focusing on reducing morbidity and mortality. Immunization budgets, disbursements, and program activities must be closely monitored and defended. Local civil society organizations (CSOs) and professional associations should be supported to contribute to national discussions on immunization and health. Opinion leaders should be informed and engaged on the value of immunization, and models for collaboration between evidence generators and policymakers should be explored to prioritize and formulate policies. Evidence on the public health value of vaccines and the importance of equitable access should be developed and disseminated. Similarly, the broad economic benefits of immunization for individuals, households, communities, and countries should be highlighted. Immunization should be included in the agendas of governing body meetings and other social, health, and economic forums. National capacity to formulate evidence-based policies should be strengthened by creating or enhancing independent advisory bodies, such as National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs). National Regulatory Agencies (NRAs), Health Sector Coordination Committees (HSCCs), and Interagency Coordination Committees (ICCs) should be more effectively integrated into immunization and disease-control programs. Regional forums and peer-to-peer exchanges should be established to share best practices and tools. Efforts should be made to engage individuals and communities on the benefits of immunization while addressing their concerns and fears through dialogue. Social media tools, mobile technologies, and internet-based platforms should be leveraged to enhance communication. Immunization should also be incorporated into basic education curricula, and incentives should be created to stimulate demand for immunization among households and health workers, while respecting their autonomy. Social research should be conducted to improve the delivery of immunization services and address the needs of diverse communities. Advocacy capacity should be built by recruiting new voices, including educators, religious leaders, social media influencers, family physicians, and community health workers. Health-care workers should be trained in effective communication techniques to address vaccine hesitancy and maintain trust. Strategies to address inequities in immunization should include adapting the Reaching Every District approach to Reaching Every Community and engaging underserved and marginalized groups to develop targeted strategies. New vaccines should be introduced into national immunization programs, and a life-course approach to immunization planning and implementation should be established. Preparedness for vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks, humanitarian crises, and conflict zones should be strengthened. Immunization programs should track individual immunization statuses using electronic databases and national identification systems. Community structures should be utilized to enhance communication and service delivery, and CSOs should be involved in community outreach and planning. New approaches to community engagement, particularly in urban and peri-urban areas, should be developed. Operational and social science research should identify successful strategies to reduce inequities and improve the quality and delivery of immunization services. Global vaccine programs focusing on eradication and elimination goals should be integrated into national immunization programs. Monitoring and surveillance systems should be strengthened to improve the quality of immunization data and its use at all administrative levels. New technologies for data collection, transmission, and analysis should be promoted. Disease surveillance systems should be expanded to include laboratory-confirmed cases for decision-making and monitoring the impact of immunization on morbidity and mortality. Cold-chain capacity and logistics should be improved, and the environmental impact of immunization supply systems should be minimized. Governments should commit to investing in immunization according to their ability to pay and the expected benefits, while exploring innovative financing mechanisms and differential pricing approaches to improve affordability for middle-income countries. Efforts should be made to secure a quality vaccine supply by building networks of regulators and suppliers, strengthening global standardization of manufacturing and regulatory processes, and harmonizing national regulatory systems. Platforms for communication between countries and manufacturers should be established to align vaccine demand with desired product profiles. Research and development (R&D) capacity in lowand middle-income countries should be enhanced, and collaboration between traditional research disciplines and new scientific fields should be promoted. Research on the fundamentals of immune responses and the characteristics of microbes should be prioritized to enable the development of new vaccines. Access to technology, know-how, and intellectual property for vaccine adjuvants should be improved, and innovative delivery mechanisms should be developed to suit country-specific needs. Finally, operational research should focus on improving delivery approaches for life-course immunization and vaccination in humanitarian emergencies and fragile states. Improved diagnostic tools for surveillance in low-income countries should also be developed to enhance immunization program efficiency and impact.
